In 1910, almost every crown in Europe belonged to a handful of families.

The King of England, the German Kaiser and the Russian Tsarina were first cousins.

Four years later, they went to war with each other.

Europe's family business — a thread 🧵👑

1/ Queen Victoria had 9 children and 42 grandchildren — and married them into nearly every court in Europe.

By 1910 her descendants sat on or next to the thrones of Britain, Germany, Russia, Spain, Norway, Sweden, Romania and Greece.

They called her "the grandmother of Europe."

2/ The map: Saxe-Coburg and Gotha in Britain, Hohenzollerns in Germany, Habsburgs in Austria-Hungary, Romanovs in Russia, Bourbons in Spain, Savoy in Italy, Bernadotte in Sweden — a French revolutionary general's family, still reigning there today.

3/ Kaiser Wilhelm II, Tsar Nicholas II and King George V knew each other as Willy, Nicky and Georgie.

George and Nicholas looked so alike that at a 1893 wedding, guests congratulated the wrong man.

4/ In July 1914, Willy and Nicky exchanged personal telegrams, cousin to cousin, trying to stop the war their own governments were sliding into.

They failed. The family group photo became a casualty list.

5/ By 1918: Hohenzollerns deposed. Habsburgs deposed. Romanovs murdered in a basement in Yekaterinburg.

The British royals survived — after quietly rebranding from "Saxe-Coburg and Gotha" to "Windsor" in 1917, because their name was the enemy's name.

6/ One family tree, three empires destroyed, one dynasty rebranded.

The 1910 map above is the last portrait of monarchical Europe — taken 4 years before the fall.
